program.name: Glorieta Gardens — Utility & Environmental Program of Work
program.owner: Glorieta Partners, Ltd. — c/o R4 GGOL GP LLC
objectives: Close the Consent Order completely with written termination.
Operate water, sewer and stormwater in conformance with design, permits and local/state regulatory obligations.
Mitigate physical risk to the property, principally flooding.
program.authorization_model: One short proposal per project; owner signature is the basis of the work; no work proceeds without an approved proposal.

fee_model.subcontracted: Cost plus 10% overhead plus 10% profit (20% total)
fee_model.recurring: Monthly professional services under annual authorization

buckets.name: Stormwater Management
buckets.posture: Stormwater Management Plan is the program's first deliverable.
buckets.tagline: The plan comes first. Everything else is written into it.
buckets.summary: We do not currently know, with engineering certainty, what the stormwater system on this property is. Not how many catch basins. Not where the pipes run, what size they are, what they are made of, or whether they are intact. There is a retention pond of unquantified capacity and a second retention area that people reference but nobody has located. Every one of those unknowns is a flood-risk unknown. So the Stormwater Management Plan is written first — not last. It establishes the design basis, the level of service the property will be held to, and the investigation program required to get there. Every project that follows is then a defined chapter of that plan rather than a standalone expense, and the plan is reissued as a final governing document once the data is in.
buckets.rationale: Flooding is the fastest way this property generates a life-safety event, a resident claim, an insurance loss, and a regulatory finding — all at once. Writing the plan first means every dollar spent afterwards has a stated purpose inside a document the owner, the engineer and the regulator all read the same way.

buckets.name: Sewer Extension
buckets.posture: Construction complete. Closing out and instrumenting.
buckets.tagline: Built. Now we hand it over — and we measure what leaves.
buckets.summary: The sanitary sewer extension is physically built. Two things remain, and they are different in kind. The first is administrative: transferring the asset to the City of Opa-Locka through a formal conveyance package. The second is operational: putting a permanent flow meter at the point where wastewater leaves the property, so that Glorieta — the system's largest single discharger — can prove exactly what it sends to the City's pump station.
buckets.rationale: Until conveyance closes, the sewer remains the owner's asset, the owner's maintenance obligation, and the owner's warranty exposure. Until the meter is in, every flow question is an argument instead of a fact.

buckets.name: Water Systems
buckets.posture: Records and file assessment approved. Balance to be proposed.
buckets.tagline: Find the pipes. Then meter, protect, and supplement them.
buckets.summary: We need to know where our water pipes are before we touch anything else. That begins with the records and file assessment — originally discussed for wastewater, now necessarily widened to every utility record we can obtain. If the records are good, we field-verify them and produce an as-built. If they are not, we run a full field verification survey. From that foundation, three construction projects follow: meter boxes (we design, permit and build; the City sets its meters), backflow prevention, and an irrigation well to serve the common areas. One further item sits at the end of this bucket, flagged for discussion rather than proposed: a non-revenue water assessment, which asks a question none of the other projects ask — how much of the water this property buys is never billed to anybody.
buckets.rationale: Any future modification — a meter box, a backflow device, a trench for stormwater — is a guess until the water system is located. Guessing is how you hit a live main. And once the system is located and metered, it becomes possible for the first time to find out what the property is paying for and not receiving.

buckets.name: Environmental Services & Regulatory Compliance
buckets.posture: Ongoing obligation. Investigation scope to be defined.
buckets.tagline: Prove what came from off-site. Close the Consent Order.
buckets.summary: Glorieta Gardens is surrounded by industrial neighbours, including junkyards. The purpose of this bucket is to establish, on the record and for the owner's own protection, whether contamination is migrating onto the property from adjacent parcels. That means an extensive file review of the surrounding properties, a plume analysis, and a monitoring well network on the boundaries — a minimum of two wells per side. Running alongside it is the standing compliance obligation: closing out the Consent Order completely and keeping water, sewer and stormwater operating in conformance with their permits at both local and state level.
buckets.rationale: If a neighbour's plume has reached this property, the owner needs to know it first, document it first, and control the narrative with DERM and the City — not learn about it during a transaction.

buckets.name: Program Management & ProjOS
buckets.tagline: One operating record. Every project, every document, every obligation.
buckets.summary: The four program buckets above are only manageable if something holds them together. APAS provides day-to-day project management for the crews on site and program-level management across all four buckets — scope control, change management, schedule, pay application review, permit tracking and regulatory correspondence. All of it is instantiated in ProjOS, so that every project carries its scope, deliverables, permits, documents and current status in one operating record the owner can open at any time.
buckets.rationale: Thirty-one projects across four systems and three regulators is not a spreadsheet problem. Without a single operating record, the owner is reconstructing the truth from email every time a question is asked.

projects.name: Stormwater Management Plan
projects.headline: Write the plan first. It defines the design basis, the level of service, and every project that follows.
projects.context: This is the program's first deliverable, and putting it first is a deliberate choice. A management plan written at the end is a filing exercise. Written at the beginning, it is the instrument that governs everything: it states what the stormwater system is meant to achieve, what standard the property will be held to, what has to be investigated to get there, and in what order. Every project after it becomes a defined chapter of a plan the owner, the engineer and the regulator all read the same way — rather than a series of separate expenses nobody can connect to each other. The plan is issued in two parts: the framework and roadmap now, and the final governing document once the investigation and modelling results are in.
scope: Issue A — Framework and roadmap. Establish the design basis, the regulatory framework, and the adopted level of service the property will be held to for each design storm.
Define the stormwater system as currently understood, and state explicitly and in writing what is not known.
Define the investigation program required to close each gap, and set the sequence and dependencies between the projects that follow.
Establish the asset identification convention so every structure and pipe carries a permanent identifier from the first day of field work.
Define the performance criteria against which the finished system will be judged.
Issue B — Final governing plan. Incorporate the investigation, survey, geotechnical, modelling and design results as they arrive.
Consolidate the complete record set: drawings, calculations, permits, test data and certifications, into one governing document.
Document the implementation sequence actually executed and the as-built configuration of the system.
Publish and maintain the plan in ProjOS as the live reference for the stormwater system.
deliverables: Stormwater Management Plan — Issue A: framework, design basis, level of service, investigation roadmap
Project sequence and dependency map
Asset identification convention
Performance criteria
Stormwater Management Plan — Issue B: final governing document with the complete record set
Live plan published in ProjOS

commercial.note: Fixed-fee professional services. Issue A and Issue B proposed separately so the owner authorises the framework without committing to the final document before the scope of investigation is known.

projects.name: Stormwater Records & File Review
projects.headline: Determine what documentation of the stormwater system actually exists before spending a dollar in the field.
projects.context: This is the least expensive project in the stormwater bucket and it governs the cost of every project after it. If usable as-builts and drainage permits exist, large parts of the field program shrink. If they do not, we know immediately that field verification is the starting point rather than the fallback — and we scope and price accordingly.

Pursue original developer, architect and engineer files, plats, easements, drainage permits and prior modification permits.
Review historical aerials and Sanborn maps to identify the original drainage configuration and any later alterations.
Specifically pursue any record of the second retention area — its location, permitted volume and whether it was ever built.
Produce a records inventory and, more importantly, a gap register: what we have, what we do not have, and what each gap costs to close in the field.
deliverables: Records inventory with source and reliability rating on every document
Gap register mapped to the field projects required to close each gap
Recommendation memo: documentation-led path or field-led path
Findings written into the Stormwater Management Plan

projects.name: CCTV Inspection of the Underground Stormwater System
projects.headline: Send a camera through every pipe, catch basin to catch basin, and find out what is actually down there.
projects.context: Nothing downstream can be designed responsibly without this. It answers, with video evidence, the questions we currently cannot answer: how many catch basins do we have, where do the pipes run, what size are they, what are they made of, are they perforated or solid, and are any of them collapsed. It is a non-intrusive condition assessment — no digging, no excavation, no disruption to residents.
scope: Locate, open and inventory every drainage structure on the property; apply the permanent numbering convention set in the Stormwater Management Plan.
Clean and jet lines as required to obtain a usable inspection.
CCTV every reach, catch basin to catch basin, with continuous video and distance-referenced logging.
Record for every reach: pipe diameter, material, joint type, slope indication, and whether the pipe is perforated or solid.
Grade structural and operational condition to NASSCO PACP standard — cracking, deformation, offset joints, root intrusion, sediment depth, and full or partial collapse.
Flag illicit connections and any discharge that does not belong in a stormwater line.
Deliver a condition-ranked defect register that drives the repair and rehabilitation priority list.
Hand the pipe network geometry directly to the survey team so the survey is verifying a known network rather than discovering one.
deliverables: Complete structure and pipe inventory with permanent IDs
Full CCTV video library, indexed and reach-referenced
NASSCO PACP condition report with defect coding
Condition-ranked defect and rehabilitation priority register
Network geometry file issued to survey

projects.headline: Produce a signed and sealed survey of the site surface and the drainage network, informed by what the camera found.
projects.context: The survey is sequenced deliberately after the CCTV rather than before it. That sequencing is what makes the survey a foundation document instead of a partial one.

Locate and elevate every drainage structure identified in the CCTV inventory — rim and invert on every pipe entering and leaving.
Tie the survey to NAVD 88 and to the Miami-Dade County control network.
Reconcile the surveyed network against the CCTV inventory and resolve every discrepancy before sealing.
Deliver signed and sealed drawings plus editable CAD, and a survey-grade base map that becomes the single geometric basis for all subsequent stormwater design.

projects.name: Geotechnical Investigation & Permeability Testing
projects.headline: Measure how fast this soil actually absorbs water, so the hydraulic model is built on site data rather than assumption.
projects.context: South Florida drainage design lives or dies on infiltration rate and seasonal high water table. Both are site-specific and both are inputs the model cannot run without. Testing at a small number of representative locations, selected once we know where the system is, gives the model defensible numbers — and defensible numbers are what survive permit review.
scope: Select boring and test locations using the survey and CCTV results, targeting proposed exfiltration and retention areas.
Advance soil borings with continuous sampling and classification.
Perform in-situ permeability testing using the Miami-Dade accepted method to establish the hydraulic conductivity value.
Establish the seasonal high water table elevation at each location.
Deliver a geotechnical report with design-ready parameters, signed and sealed.

Seasonal high water table elevations

projects.name: Retention Pond Survey
projects.headline: Establish the pond's real shape, depth and current storage volume — above and below the waterline.
projects.context: The retention pond is the property's primary stormwater storage asset, and we do not know its current capacity. Sediment accumulates slowly and silently; the pond looks unchanged from the bank while the storage inside it disappears. A bathymetric and topographic survey establishes what capacity exists today against what capacity was permitted, and that difference is the dredging case.
scope: Topographic survey of the pond banks, top of bank, side slopes and control structure.
Bathymetric survey of the pond bottom on a defined grid, capturing the sediment surface.
Probe to establish the depth of accumulated sediment and the original design bottom where recoverable.
Survey and document the outfall control structure, including weir elevations and orifice dimensions.
Compute the current stage-storage relationship and compare it against the permitted design storage.
deliverables: Pond topographic and bathymetric survey
Sediment thickness map
Current versus permitted stage-storage curve
Control structure documentation

commercial.fee_basis: Subcontracted at cost plus 10% overhead and 10% profit; APAS administers

projects.name: Digital Terrain Model & Dredge Volume Determination
projects.headline: Turn the pond survey into a three-dimensional model and compute exactly how much material has to come out.
projects.context: Dredging is priced by the cubic yard. Without a computed volume, the owner is exposed to open-ended quantities and change orders. A digital terrain model built from the survey produces a defensible quantity before anyone mobilises, and it becomes the basis for the bid, for the disposal estimate, and for measuring the contractor's completion.
scope: Build a digital terrain model of the existing sediment surface and of the target design bottom.
Compute cut volumes between the two surfaces, with contingency banding.
Produce dredge limit drawings and target elevation contours for the contractor.
Establish the measurement and verification method for confirming completion and final quantities.
Model the post-dredge stage-storage curve to confirm the storage volume recovered.
deliverables: Digital terrain model (existing and design surfaces)
Computed dredge volume with contingency band
Dredge limit and target elevation drawings
Measurement and verification protocol
Post-dredge stage-storage curve

commercial.note: Fixed-fee professional services — analysis and drawing production from existing survey data.

projects.name: Dredged Material Characterization, Profiling & Disposal
projects.headline: Sample and profile the sediment before it moves, so it goes to a facility that will legally accept it.
projects.context: This has to happen before dredging, not after. Sediment from a pond adjacent to industrial neighbours cannot be assumed clean. Waste profiling determines the disposal pathway and the disposal cost, and those two facts can swing the dredging budget by a wide margin. Profiling first also protects the owner from the worst case in this kind of work: material excavated, staged on site, and then found to be unacceptable at the receiving facility.
scope: Develop a sampling and analysis plan appropriate to the pond and the surrounding land uses.
Collect representative sediment samples across the pond footprint and at depth.
Laboratory analysis for the contaminants of concern indicated by the adjacent land uses, including metals and petroleum constituents.
Prepare the waste profile and obtain written acceptance from the receiving facility before dredging begins.
Determine the disposal pathway and confirm hauling, manifesting and chain of custody requirements.
Manage transport and disposal during dredging, with full manifest documentation retained for the compliance record.
deliverables: Sampling and analysis plan
Laboratory analytical results
Approved waste profile and written facility acceptance
Disposal pathway determination memo
Complete manifest and chain of custody file

commercial.fee_basis: Lump sum professional services + subcontracted work at cost plus 10% overhead and 10% profit
commercial.note: APAS professional services on a fixed fee; laboratory, hauling and disposal procured and administered by APAS. Disposal cost is governed by the characterization result — which is precisely why it is determined early and cheaply.

projects.name: Retention Pond Dredging
projects.headline: Remove the accumulated sediment and restore the pond to its design storage volume.
projects.context: This is the physical recovery of storage capacity the property has lost to sedimentation. It is a construction project with a measured quantity, a defined target elevation and a verification survey at completion — not an open-ended clean-out.

Mobilise, install turbidity and erosion controls, and establish the dewatering and staging area.
Dredge to the design bottom elevation within the defined limits.
Dewater the removed material to a transportable moisture content.
Restore banks and side slopes; stabilise and re-vegetate disturbed areas, including the littoral zone.
Post-dredge verification survey confirming target elevations and the storage volume recovered.

projects.name: Comprehensive Hydrologic & Hydraulic Model
projects.headline: Model the whole property against the 5-year, 25-year and 100-year storms and find out where the water goes.
projects.context: This is the analytical core of the stormwater bucket. Every field project before it exists to feed this model, and every design project after it is dictated by its results. It answers the question the owner actually cares about: in a real storm, does water enter the buildings, and are the streets passable. Modelling three return periods separates a nuisance event from a life-safety event and tells us which improvements are required rather than merely desirable.
scope: Build the model from the survey base map, the CCTV network geometry, the geotechnical permeability values and the pond stage-storage curve.
Calibrate against observed flooding history on the property where records or resident reports exist.
Run the 5-year, 25-year and 100-year design storms for the applicable durations.
Evaluate two protection criteria explicitly and separately: finished floor elevation protection for every building, and roadway passability for emergency access.
Identify every deficiency — undersized pipes, insufficient storage, inadequate pumping, low points and overland flow paths.
Test improvement scenarios and quantify the flood-risk reduction each one buys.
Determine whether the pond and pipe network alone can meet the required level of service, or whether supplemental features are needed.
Write the results into the Stormwater Management Plan as the governing design basis.
deliverables: Calibrated hydrologic and hydraulic model
Flood maps and inundation depths for each return period
Finished floor and roadway risk assessment by building and by street
Deficiency register with hydraulic cause identified
Improvement scenario comparison with risk reduction quantified
Determination on the need for supplemental features

commercial.note: Fixed-fee professional services — model build, calibration, three-storm analysis and scenario testing.

projects.name: Stormwater Lift Station — Adequacy Assessment, Siting & Design
projects.headline: Determine whether the pumping capacity serving the pond is adequate, whether it is in the right place, and design what it should be.
projects.context: A retention pond only performs if what leaves it can leave fast enough. This project evaluates the existing pumping arrangement against modelled demand, tests whether its location relative to the pond is hydraulically correct, and produces a design for whatever the answer requires — rerating, relocating, or replacing.
scope: Assess the existing lift station: condition, capacity, controls, power supply and reliability.
Evaluate its location relative to the retention pond and to the modelled inflow points.
Determine required firm capacity against the modelled design storms.
Evaluate siting alternatives where relocation is indicated.
Produce design drawings and specifications for the selected configuration, including wet well, pumps, controls, standby power and telemetry.
Establish the permitting pathway and prepare permit-ready documents.
deliverables: Adequacy and condition assessment report
Siting alternatives evaluation with recommendation
Signed and sealed design drawings and specifications
Permit-ready submittal package

projects.name: Retention Pond Design & Reconfiguration
projects.headline: Design the pond to the storage volume the model requires, not the volume it happens to have.
projects.context: Once the model states the storage volume this property needs in order to be protected in a design storm, the pond has to be designed to deliver it. That may mean deepening, expanding the footprint, reshaping side slopes for safety and maintenance access, or rebuilding the control structure.

Design side slopes, safety shelf, littoral zone and maintenance access.
Design the outfall control structure — weir, orifice and discharge rate — to the permitted allowable discharge.
Integrate with the lift station design and confirm combined performance.
Prepare permit-ready drawings, calculations and specifications.

Permit submittal package

projects.name: Site Regrading & Recontouring — Design, Permit & Construct
projects.headline: Reshape the ground so that water goes where the model says it should go.
projects.context: The model will identify low points, reverse slopes and blocked overland flow paths that no pipe can fix. Regrading is how a property is made to drain by gravity before any mechanical system is asked to help. This is the largest construction item in the program and is scoped, phased and priced directly from the model results.
scope: Design regrading and recontouring to achieve the drainage patterns and hydraulic capacity established by the model.
Set finished floor protection and roadway crown elevations to the adopted level of service.
Design conveyance improvements — swales, inlets, pipe upsizing — where the model identifies capacity deficiency.
Permit through Miami-Dade DERM, SFWMD and the City of Opa-Locka.
Phase construction to maintain resident access, parking and emergency vehicle circulation throughout.
Construct, with survey verification of finished grades against design.
Restore paving, landscaping and site features.

Approved permits
Phased construction plan with resident access maintained
Constructed improvements with as-built survey verification
Record drawings issued into the Stormwater Management Plan

projects.name: Supplemental Stormwater Features — Exfiltration Trench & the Second Retention Area
projects.headline: If the model says the pond and pipes are not enough, add capacity — and finally settle the question of the second retention area.
projects.context: This project is deliberately conditional. It is triggered only if the hydraulic model demonstrates that the primary system cannot meet the required level of service. Two options are on the table. The first is an exfiltration trench system, which is the standard Miami-Dade answer and depends directly on the permeability values from the geotechnical work. The second is the second retention area — a feature everybody on this property references and nobody has located. That ambiguity is itself a liability, and this project closes it: we either find it, confirm it, and restore it to function, or we establish on the record that it does not exist.
scope: Locate and confirm the second retention area through records, historical aerials, geophysical survey and field investigation.
If found: assess its condition, permitted status and residual storage capacity, and determine whether restoration is viable and cost-effective.
If not found: document the investigation and formally close the question so it stops appearing as an open assumption in every future analysis.
Design an exfiltration trench system sized to the residual storage deficit, using the measured hydraulic conductivity from the geotechnical work.
Compare the two options on capacity delivered, cost, permitability and long-term maintenance burden.
Permit and construct the selected option.
deliverables: Second retention area investigation report — located and assessed, or formally closed out
Exfiltration trench design and calculations
Options comparison with recommendation
Permits and constructed improvements

commercial.fee_basis: Lump sum professional services + subcontracted work at cost plus 10% overhead and 10% profit
commercial.note: Conditional — proposed only if the model identifies a residual storage deficit. Investigation and design on a fixed fee; construction procured and administered by APAS.

projects.context: A management plan describes the system. An operations plan runs it. This is the document that survives staff turnover: who inspects what, how often, what triggers a response, what gets recorded, and what gets reported to whom. Set inspection frequencies, cleaning cycles and sediment removal triggers, so storage loss is caught early rather than rediscovered in a decade.
Establish pre-storm readiness and post-storm response procedures.

Establish record-keeping, evidence retention and the annual system condition review.
Define performance monitoring, alarm thresholds and escalation paths.
Build the operating record into ProjOS with scheduled tasks, evidence capture and automatic compliance reporting.

projects.name: Master Effluent Flow Meter at the Property Discharge Point
projects.headline: Install a permanent flow meter where wastewater leaves the property, so total discharge to the City pump station is a measured fact.
projects.context: Glorieta Gardens is the largest single discharger into this pump station. Today, the volume leaving the property is inferred rather than measured. That is a problem in three directions at once: it makes infiltration and inflow impossible to isolate, it leaves billing and capacity allocation open to dispute, and it means any compliance question about what we discharge has no defensible answer. A meter at the exit resolves all three.
scope: Confirm the single point of discharge from the property to the City's collection system and verify there is no secondary or bypass connection.
Design a permanent metering structure — vault or dedicated manhole — sized and located for safe, permanent access and for accurate hydraulic conditions.

glossary.technical: A permitted stormwater impoundment designed to capture a defined runoff volume and release it primarily by infiltration into the ground and evaporation, rather than by discharging it downstream. Its performance is expressed as a stage-storage relationship — how many cubic feet of water it holds at each water-surface elevation — and it is regulated against a permitted storage volume and an allowable discharge rate.
glossary.plain_english: A shallow basin that holds rainwater and lets it soak into the ground instead of running off the property. Think of it as the property's bathtub: rain fills it during a storm, and it drains slowly afterwards. Its whole value is how much water it can hold. Over the years, dirt and sediment settle on the bottom and quietly steal that capacity — the pond looks the same from the bank, but it holds less than it used to.
glossary.why_it_matters: This pond is the property's primary storage asset, and nobody currently knows how much storage is left in it. That number is the difference between a storm that drains and a storm that floods.

glossary.technical: A detention facility temporarily stores runoff and releases it downstream at a controlled rate through an outfall structure. A retention facility holds the volume and disposes of it on site through infiltration. Most South Florida systems operate as a hybrid: retention up to a design volume, with controlled detention discharge above it.
glossary.plain_english: Detention slows water down and lets it out. Retention holds water and lets it soak away. One manages the rate, the other manages the volume — and a well-designed pond usually does both.

glossary.technical: An inlet structure — typically a concrete box with a grate or curb opening — that receives surface runoff and conveys it into the underground piped drainage network. It also acts as a sediment sump, trapping solids before they enter the pipes.
glossary.plain_english: The grate in the parking lot that water disappears into. Underneath it is a concrete box connected to a pipe. It is also the property's first line of defense against debris — which is exactly why it fills with sediment and stops working if nobody cleans it.

glossary.technical: Closed-circuit television inspection: a self-propelled or winched camera is run through a pipe reach, producing continuous distance-referenced video. Output includes pipe diameter, material, joint condition, slope indication, and coded structural and operational defects.
glossary.plain_english: A camera on wheels driven through the pipe, recording the whole way. It is the only way to see the condition of a buried pipe without digging it up — and it answers questions no drawing can: is the pipe cracked, is it full of sediment, has it collapsed.

glossary.technical: Pipeline Assessment Certification Program — the North American industry standard for coding pipe defects observed during CCTV inspection. It produces a consistent, numerically graded condition score for each defect and each reach.
glossary.plain_english: A standard scoring system for pipe defects, so 'bad condition' means the same thing to every engineer, contractor and regulator who reads the report. Without it, a condition assessment is one inspector's opinion.

glossary.technical: The invert is the elevation of the inside bottom of a pipe where it enters or leaves a structure. The rim is the elevation of the structure's top at grade. The difference between inverts across a reach establishes the pipe's slope, and therefore whether it drains by gravity.
glossary.plain_english: The rim is the top of the manhole you see. The invert is the bottom of the pipe below it. The difference between the inverts at each end of a pipe tells you which way the water actually flows — and whether it flows at all.

glossary.technical: A perforated pipe bedded in clean gravel and wrapped in filter fabric, installed below the water table, that distributes stormwater into the surrounding soil. In Miami-Dade it is designed under Chapter 24 criteria using the site's measured hydraulic conductivity.
glossary.plain_english: A gravel-filled trench with a slotted pipe running through it, buried underground. Water enters the pipe and seeps out sideways into the soil. It is the standard South Florida way to add drainage capacity when there is no room for another pond — but it only works if the soil actually absorbs water, which is why we test the soil first.

glossary.technical: A measured soil property expressing the rate at which water moves through a saturated soil, typically reported in cubic feet per second per square foot per foot of head. It is the governing design input for exfiltration and retention sizing.
glossary.plain_english: How fast water soaks into the ground here, measured rather than assumed. It is the single number that decides how big a drainage feature has to be. Guess it high and the system floods; guess it low and you overbuild by hundreds of thousands of dollars.

glossary.technical: The highest elevation the groundwater surface is expected to reach in a normal wet season. It sets the lower design limit for infiltration systems, since storage below the water table is unavailable.
glossary.plain_english: In the wet season the groundwater rises. Anything buried below that level is already sitting in water and cannot absorb any more. It is the floor under every drainage design in South Florida.

glossary.technical: A curve relating water-surface elevation (stage) in a basin to the volume of water stored at that elevation. It is derived from survey and is the fundamental input to routing calculations.
glossary.plain_english: A simple chart: at each water level in the pond, how many gallons is it holding. It is how you convert 'the pond looks full' into an actual number you can design against.

glossary.technical: Survey of the submerged bottom surface of a water body on a defined grid, typically by sonar or direct probing, referenced to a vertical datum. Paired with probing to distinguish the accumulated sediment surface from the original design bottom.
glossary.plain_english: Surveying the bottom of the pond, underwater. A normal survey stops at the waterline; this one keeps going. It is the only way to find out how much sediment has built up and how much storage that sediment has taken away.

glossary.technical: A three-dimensional surface model built from survey points, used to compute volumes between an existing surface and a proposed design surface.
glossary.plain_english: A 3-D computer model of the ground and the pond bottom. Its practical use here is arithmetic: subtract the design bottom from the current bottom and you get exactly how many cubic yards of muck have to come out — before anybody bids the job.

glossary.technical: Mechanical or hydraulic removal of accumulated sediment from a basin to restore design storage volume, followed by dewatering, transport and disposal of the removed material.
glossary.plain_english: Digging the accumulated muck out of the bottom of the pond so it can hold water again. It is priced by the cubic yard, which is why knowing the volume before you start is worth more than it costs to find out.

glossary.technical: Laboratory characterization of a material against the acceptance criteria of a receiving facility, establishing whether it classifies as clean fill, solid waste, or regulated waste, and determining lawful disposal pathway, manifesting and transport requirements.
glossary.plain_english: Testing the muck before you dig it up, to find out where it is legally allowed to go. This matters enormously to cost: clean fill is cheap to dispose of, contaminated material is not. It also avoids the worst outcome in this kind of work — excavating it, stockpiling it on site, and then finding out nobody will take it.

glossary.technical: A wet well with pumps, controls and discharge piping that moves water from a lower elevation to a higher one where gravity flow is not available. Sizing is expressed as firm capacity — the flow deliverable with the largest pump out of service.
glossary.plain_english: A pit with pumps in it. Where the ground is too flat for water to drain away on its own, you pump it. A retention pond only performs if what comes in can also get out — and on a flat site, that usually means pumps.

glossary.technical: A computational model that generates runoff from a design rainfall event (hydrology) and routes it through the pipe network, storage and control structures (hydraulics), producing water-surface elevations, flow rates and inundation extents over time.
glossary.plain_english: A computer simulation of what happens on this property when it rains hard. You put in the real pipes, the real ground shape and the real soil, then run a storm through it and watch where the water goes and how deep it gets. It is the difference between an opinion about flooding and an answer.

glossary.technical: A synthetic rainfall event of specified depth and duration with a stated annual exceedance probability. A 25-year storm has a 4% chance of being equalled or exceeded in any given year; a 100-year storm, 1%.
glossary.plain_english: A '100-year storm' does not mean once a century — it means a 1-in-100 chance of happening in any given year, which is roughly a 1-in-4 chance over a 30-year hold. Designing to three different storms tells you three different things: the 5-year is nuisance flooding, the 25-year is the regulatory standard, and the 100-year is whether people's homes take water.

glossary.technical: The elevation of the lowest habitable floor of a structure, referenced to a vertical datum. Flood protection criteria are expressed as required freeboard between the modeled peak water-surface elevation and this elevation.
glossary.plain_english: How high the floor of an apartment sits above the ground. It is the line that separates an inconvenient storm from an insurance claim, a displaced resident and a lawsuit. Every flood number in this program is ultimately measured against it.

glossary.technical: The adopted performance standard a drainage system is designed to meet — typically expressed as no habitable-floor flooding in a stated design storm and passable roadways for emergency access in another.
glossary.plain_english: The standard you decide to build to, stated out loud. 'No water in the buildings in a 25-year storm, streets passable for a fire truck in a 100-year storm' is a level of service. Without one, nobody can say whether the system is good enough.

glossary.technical: The surface route runoff follows when piped capacity is exceeded. Preserving intentional overland flow paths is a standard resilience measure for events beyond the piped design storm.
glossary.plain_english: Where the water goes once the pipes are full. Every site has these paths whether they were designed or not — the question is whether they run harmlessly to the pond or straight through somebody's front door.

glossary.technical: The outfall structure that governs discharge from a basin. A weir is an overflow crest controlling higher stages; an orifice is a fixed opening controlling low-stage discharge. Their dimensions and elevations set the permitted discharge rate.
glossary.plain_english: The concrete box at the pond outlet with a notch and a hole in it. The hole controls the slow everyday drainage; the notch handles the overflow in a big storm. Those two dimensions are what the permit actually regulates — change them and you have changed the permit.

glossary.technical: A shallow vegetated bench around the perimeter of a pond, typically required by permit. It provides water quality treatment through plant uptake and functions as a safety shelf preventing immediate drop-off at the water's edge.
glossary.plain_english: The shallow planted shelf around the edge of the pond. It cleans the water and, just as importantly, means someone who steps in at the bank does not go straight over their head.

glossary.technical: A measure of water clarity reduced by suspended particles, regulated during in-water construction. Exceedances above background at a compliance boundary trigger work stoppage.
glossary.plain_english: How muddy the water is. During dredging, regulators watch it closely — cloud up the water beyond the allowed limit and the job stops until it clears.

glossary.technical: North American Vertical Datum of 1988 — the standard vertical reference for elevations in the United States. All flood, floor and invert elevations must share a single datum to be comparable.
glossary.plain_english: The common yardstick for elevation. If the survey, the flood maps and the building floors are measured from different starting points, none of the numbers can be compared — and in South Florida, a foot of error is the whole margin.

glossary.technical: Perforated pipe has openings along its barrel and is intended to exchange water with the surrounding soil, as in an exfiltration system. Solid pipe is watertight and intended purely for conveyance.
glossary.plain_english: Slotted pipe is meant to leak — it is drainage by design. Solid pipe is meant to carry water from A to B without losing any. Knowing which is which underground completely changes how the system behaves, and it is one of the first things the camera tells us.

glossary.technical: Any connection to the storm sewer conveying a non-stormwater discharge. Detection and elimination is a mandatory minimum control measure under the NPDES MS4 program.
glossary.plain_english: Something plumbed into the storm drain that has no business being there — a sink, a wash bay, a sewer line crossed into the wrong pipe. It goes straight to the environment untreated, and finding one is a regulatory obligation, not an option.

glossary.technical: Reshaping site topography to establish positive drainage toward intended collection points, correct reverse slopes and low points, and set roadway crown and swale elevations to the adopted level of service.
glossary.plain_english: Reshaping the ground so water runs where you want it to. No pipe can fix a low spot that has nowhere to drain. This is the unglamorous work that makes everything else function — and on a flat site it is usually the biggest single item.

glossary.technical: A shallow vegetated channel that conveys and infiltrates runoff, providing both conveyance and water quality treatment.
glossary.plain_english: A shallow grassy ditch that carries and soaks up rainwater. Cheap, low-maintenance, and effective — as long as nobody parks on it or fills it in.

glossary.technical: The governing engineering document for a site's stormwater system: design basis, adopted level of service, system inventory, modeling results, drawings, calculations, permits, test data and the implementation sequence.
glossary.plain_english: The one document that explains the whole stormwater system — what it is, what it is designed to do, and what has to be built to get it there. Everything else in this bucket either feeds it or comes out of it. It is written first so that every project after it has a defined place in a plan, rather than being a standalone expense nobody can connect to anything.

glossary.technical: The operational counterpart to the management plan: inspection and maintenance procedures by asset class, frequencies and triggers, pre-storm and post-storm protocols, the regulatory reporting calendar with assigned responsibility, and the evidence retention regime.
glossary.plain_english: The management plan describes the system. The operations plan runs it — who checks what, how often, what to do when a storm is coming, and what gets written down. It is the document that survives staff turnover.

glossary.technical: Municipal Separate Storm Sewer System permit issued under the National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System of the Clean Water Act. It imposes minimum control measures including illicit discharge detection, good housekeeping, inspection and annual reporting.
glossary.plain_english: The federal permit that governs what the storm drain system is allowed to send to public waters. It comes with standing duties — inspect, document, report — and those duties do not pause because nobody is asking.

glossary.technical: The South Florida Water Management District permit governing site stormwater management: permitted storage volume, allowable discharge rate, treatment volume and system configuration. Modifications to the permitted system require permit modification.
glossary.plain_english: The state water district's permit for how this property handles rain. It fixes how much water the site must hold and how fast it may release. Change the pond or the outfall and you are changing the permit, whether you filed for it or not.

glossary.technical: The Miami-Dade County Environmental Protection Code, administered by DERM. It governs drainage design criteria, exfiltration sizing, cross-connection control, well permitting and contamination assessment within the county.
glossary.plain_english: The county's environmental rulebook. Locally it usually bites harder than the state rules, and DERM enforces it.

glossary.technical: Miami-Dade County Department of Regulatory and Economic Resources, Division of Environmental Resources Management — the county environmental regulator for drainage, wells, contamination assessment and cross-connection control.
glossary.plain_english: The county environmental agency. They permit the wells, they review the drainage, and they are the ones who decide whether a contamination question is closed.

glossary.technical: Florida Department of Environmental Protection — the state environmental regulator, with jurisdiction over sewer certifications, contamination assessment and cleanup under Chapter 62-780 F.A.C., and solid waste.
glossary.plain_english: The state environmental agency. County and state both have a say here, and they do not always ask for the same thing.

glossary.technical: A binding, negotiated enforcement instrument between a regulator and a respondent, enumerating specific corrective actions, deadlines and reporting obligations. It terminates only upon documented completion of every enumerated action and written release by the agency.
glossary.plain_english: A legal agreement with the regulator listing exactly what has to be fixed and by when. It does not expire on its own and it does not quietly go away — it closes when every item is done, documented, and released in writing. Until then it stays attached to the property.

glossary.technical: A sanitary collection system in which flow is conveyed by gravity along a continuous downward slope, without pumping, from service laterals through mains to a receiving pump station or treatment facility.
glossary.plain_english: Sewer pipe laid on a constant downhill slope so waste flows on its own, no pumps. Simple and reliable — provided the slope is right, which is exactly what the record drawings and CCTV have to prove.

glossary.technical: The formal legal and administrative transfer of a constructed utility to the operating public utility, comprising engineering certifications, record drawings, testing evidence, warranties, title instruments, bills of sale and performance security, culminating in written acceptance.
glossary.plain_english: Handing the finished sewer over to the City so it becomes their pipe to own, operate, fix and pay for. Until that transfer is accepted in writing, it is still the owner's asset, the owner's repair bill and the owner's liability.

glossary.technical: Extraneous water entering a sanitary system: infiltration is groundwater entering through defects and joints; inflow is stormwater entering through direct connections and manhole covers. Both consume conveyance and treatment capacity and are billed as sewage.
glossary.plain_english: Groundwater and rainwater leaking into the sewer where they do not belong. You end up paying to move and treat clean water as if it were sewage. On a wet site, it can be a large share of the bill — and you cannot manage it until you can measure it.

glossary.technical: A permanent metering installation at a point of discharge, measuring flow continuously with time-stamped data logging and telemetry, calibrated to a certified accuracy and used for billing, capacity allocation and I&I quantification.
glossary.plain_english: A meter on the pipe leaving the property, recording continuously. It turns 'we think we discharge about this much' into a number nobody can argue with — for billing, for capacity, and for proving how much of the flow is actually rainwater.

glossary.technical: The characteristic 24-hour pattern of sanitary flow, showing morning and evening peaks and a pre-dawn minimum. Elevated pre-dawn minimum flow, when occupied-building discharge should be near zero, is the classic signature of groundwater infiltration.
glossary.plain_english: Sewer flow follows daily life — it spikes when people shower and cook, and drops to almost nothing at 3 a.m. If it is not near zero at 3 a.m., that extra water is groundwater leaking in. It is one of the clearest diagnostics there is, and it needs a meter to see it.

glossary.technical: A percentage of each progress payment withheld by the owner and released on defined milestones — typically part at substantial completion and the balance after final warranty inspection — as security for completion and defect correction.
glossary.plain_english: Money held back from the contractor until the work is finished and proven. It is the last real leverage anyone has once the crews have left the site.

glossary.technical: An executed instrument by which a contractor, subcontractor or supplier relinquishes lien rights against the property for work performed or materials supplied through a stated date, in exchange for payment.
glossary.plain_english: A signed document saying 'I have been paid and I will not put a lien on this property.' Without a complete set, a paid-in-full job can still surface as a claim against the title later.

glossary.technical: The point at which work is sufficiently complete that the owner may occupy or use it for its intended purpose. It starts the warranty period and triggers partial retainage release.
glossary.plain_english: The date the system is usable, even if small items remain. It matters because it starts the warranty clock — which is why the date has to be established and documented, not assumed.

glossary.technical: Drawings signed and sealed by the engineer or surveyor depicting the facility as actually constructed, including field changes, with horizontal locations and vertical elevations verified by survey.
glossary.plain_english: Drawings of what was actually built, not what was drawn beforehand. Those two things are never quite the same. Sealed as-builts are what the City accepts at conveyance, and what anyone digging here in ten years will rely on.

glossary.technical: The licensed professional engineer who takes professional responsibility for the design and issues the sealed certifications a permitting authority requires for acceptance.
glossary.plain_english: The licensed engineer whose seal and license stand behind the design. Certain documents cannot be issued by anyone else, which makes their availability a real scheduling dependency.

glossary.technical: A Florida-licensed PSM authorized to sign and seal boundary, topographic and as-built surveys. Sealed surveys are required for permitting and utility conveyance.
glossary.plain_english: The licensed surveyor whose seal makes a survey official. An unsealed sketch is useful internally; only a sealed survey is accepted by a permitting agency.

glossary.technical: Financial security posted to the receiving utility at conveyance — commonly a percentage of total construction cost plus a fixed final-obligations cash bond — guaranteeing correction of defects during the acceptance and warranty period.
glossary.plain_english: A bond or deposit the City holds after taking over the system, in case something fails soon after handover. It is a real cash requirement at conveyance and is handled by the owner and counsel, not by APAS.

glossary.technical: A mechanical assembly preventing reverse flow from a customer's system into the public potable distribution main. Device class — reduced pressure zone (RPZ) or double check valve assembly (DCVA) — is selected by hazard classification, and certified annual testing is mandatory.
glossary.plain_english: A one-way valve on the water service that stops water from flowing backwards into the public drinking water main if pressure drops. The installation is straightforward. The part people miss is that every device must be tested and certified by a licensed tester every single year, forever — and a missed test is a violation even if the device is perfect.

glossary.technical: Water treated to drinking water standards and delivered through the public distribution system, subject to Safe Drinking Water Act and F.A.C. 62-555 requirements.
glossary.plain_english: Treated drinking water. It is the most expensive water on the property, which is why using it to irrigate grass is worth reconsidering.

glossary.technical: The below-grade enclosure and service setting that houses a water meter, constructed to utility standard with the service piping and appurtenances required for the utility to install and read its meter.
glossary.plain_english: The concrete or plastic box in the ground that a water meter sits in. We build the box and the setting to the City's standard; the City brings and installs the meter itself. Sequencing that handover is most of the work — a box that is not ready on the day the City arrives costs weeks.

glossary.technical: Non-destructive designation of buried utilities using electromagnetic induction and ground-penetrating radar, followed where required by vacuum excavation (potholing) to physically verify horizontal position, depth, diameter and material.
glossary.plain_english: Finding buried pipes without digging up the whole site — first with instruments from the surface, then by carefully exposing a few specific spots to confirm what is actually there. It costs a fraction of what hitting a live main costs.

glossary.technical: Small-diameter test excavation, typically by vacuum, exposing a buried utility to directly measure depth, diameter, material and condition without damaging it.
glossary.plain_english: Digging one small careful hole to physically see the pipe and confirm what the instruments said. A handful of these turns a probable location into a known one.

glossary.technical: A permitted non-potable supply well drawing from the surficial aquifer for landscape irrigation, requiring DERM well construction permitting and SFWMD water use authorization, and physically separated from the potable system with backflow protection.
glossary.plain_english: A well that pumps groundwater for watering the grounds, instead of paying for treated drinking water to do it. It lowers the water bill, takes irrigation volume off the meters, and keeps a non-drinking use physically separate from the drinking water system.

glossary.technical: The shallow unconfined water-bearing formation beneath the site — in this area the Biscayne Aquifer — from which non-potable supply is typically drawn and within which contaminant migration occurs.
glossary.plain_english: The shallow groundwater under the property. It is where an irrigation well draws from — and it is also the path any contamination from a neighbouring property would travel along.

glossary.technical: Florida's statutory one-call underground utility notification system. Excavators must notify before digging so member utilities can mark their facilities. Notification does not locate private on-site utilities.
glossary.plain_english: The call-before-you-dig service. Worth knowing: it marks the utilities owned by the public utilities, not the private pipes inside a property like this one. Those are ours to find — which is exactly why the as-built work matters.

glossary.technical: A defined body of contaminated groundwater migrating from a source in the direction of the hydraulic gradient. It is characterised by its constituents, concentration distribution, extent and rate and direction of movement.
glossary.plain_english: A slow-moving underground stain in the groundwater, spreading outward from wherever it leaked. It travels with the groundwater, so it moves in one predictable direction — which means you can work out in advance which side of a property it would arrive on, and put your wells there.

glossary.technical: The slope of the groundwater surface, determining direction and rate of flow. Established by synoptic water-level measurements across three or more wells referenced to a common datum.
glossary.plain_english: Groundwater flows downhill too — just very slowly, and the hill is invisible. Measuring the water level in several wells on the same day tells you which way it is heading, and therefore where anything dissolved in it is heading.

glossary.technical: A small-diameter cased and screened well installed to permit measurement of groundwater elevation and collection of representative groundwater samples at a defined depth interval.
glossary.plain_english: A narrow permanent pipe into the groundwater that lets you measure the water level and take samples from the same spot, year after year. One sample is a data point; the same well sampled repeatedly is a trend — and the trend is what actually answers the question.

glossary.technical: Upgradient wells lie hydraulically above the area of interest and establish background quality. Downgradient wells lie below it and detect contaminants migrating from an upgradient source.
glossary.plain_english: Upstream and downstream, in groundwater terms. You need both: the upstream well tells you what the water looks like before it reaches the property, and the downstream well tells you what changed. Without the first, you cannot prove the second came from somewhere else.

glossary.technical: The specific analytes selected for laboratory analysis based on documented historical use and known releases at identified source properties, rather than a generic panel.
glossary.plain_english: The specific substances worth testing for, chosen from what the neighbouring properties actually did and actually spilled. Testing for the right short list beats testing for everything — it is cheaper and the results mean more.

glossary.technical: Numerical concentration standards established under Chapter 62-780 F.A.C. against which detected groundwater concentrations are compared to determine whether further assessment or remediation is required.
glossary.plain_english: The state's published thresholds. Below them, a detection is generally a non-issue; above them, obligations start. It is the line that turns a lab number into a decision.

glossary.technical: The documented, unbroken record of sample possession and transfer from collection through laboratory analysis, required for analytical results to be defensible.
glossary.plain_english: The paper trail proving a sample went straight from the well to the lab without being tampered with. Without it, a result that favours you is not usable when it counts.

glossary.technical: Historical fire insurance maps and sequential aerial photography used to reconstruct prior land use, identify former structures, tanks and operations, and establish the temporal history of potential contamination sources.
glossary.plain_english: Old insurance maps and aerial photographs going back decades. They show what used to be on the neighbouring land — the tanks, the workshops, the wrecking yards — long before anyone was required to report a spill.

glossary.technical: The Florida Administrative Code rule governing contaminated site cleanup criteria — assessment, risk evaluation, cleanup target levels and closure pathways including No Further Action.
glossary.plain_english: The state rulebook for contaminated sites: how you investigate, what counts as clean, and how a site formally gets closed out.

glossary.technical: The difference between system input volume and billed authorized consumption, expressed as a volume and as a percentage of input. It comprises unbilled authorized consumption, apparent losses — metering inaccuracy, data-handling error and unauthorized consumption — and real losses from mains, service connections and storage.
glossary.plain_english: Water you paid for that nobody paid you for. It arrives at the property, and then some of it never shows up on a bill — because it leaked out of a pipe, because a meter is reading low, or because it was used somewhere nobody is accounting for. On a property this size, the gap between what comes in and what gets billed is usually wider than anyone expects.
glossary.why_it_matters: Glorieta buys water from the City and is about to install a full set of meters. That combination is exactly when a water balance is worth doing — it is the only way to find out whether the property is paying every month for water that is running into the ground.

glossary.technical: The standard AWWA M36 accounting framework reconciling system input volume against authorized consumption and losses, disaggregating apparent from real losses and producing validated performance indicators including the Infrastructure Leakage Index.
glossary.plain_english: A structured ledger for water: everything that came in on one side, everything that can be accounted for on the other, and a disciplined method for explaining the difference. It being the industry-standard method matters — the result is comparable, defensible and recognised by anyone who later reviews it.

glossary.technical: Non-physical losses: customer meter under-registration, systematic data transfer and billing errors, and unauthorized consumption. The water is delivered and used, but not correctly measured or billed.
glossary.plain_english: Water that did get used, but never got counted properly — an old meter reading low, a billing record nobody entered, a connection nobody knows about. These are usually the cheapest losses to fix, because the fix is a meter or a spreadsheet rather than a trench.

glossary.technical: Physical losses from the pressurised system: background leakage, reported and unreported bursts on mains and service connections, and storage overflow. Quantified against the theoretical minimum for a system of the same length, connection count and pressure.
glossary.plain_english: Water genuinely leaking out of the pipes into the ground. Most of it never surfaces — it seeps away quietly, day and night, for years. You pay for every gallon of it.

glossary.technical: The ratio of current annual real losses to unavoidable annual real losses. An ILI of 1.0 represents the technical minimum achievable for that system's length, connections and operating pressure; higher values indicate recoverable leakage.
glossary.plain_english: A single score for how leaky this system is compared with how leaky it would be in perfect condition. A score near 1 means there is nothing worth chasing. A high score means there is real money running into the ground — and it tells you that before you spend anything digging.

glossary.technical: The lowest continuous flow rate recorded across a 24-hour cycle, typically between 2 and 4 a.m. when legitimate consumption is at its minimum. Residual flow above estimated night-time use is a direct indicator of leakage.
glossary.plain_english: At three in the morning almost nobody is using water. Whatever is still flowing at that hour is mostly leaking. It is one of the simplest and most powerful leak indicators there is, and it needs nothing more than a meter that logs continuously.

glossary.technical: A hydraulically discrete zone of a distribution system with metered inflow, allowing losses to be quantified and localised within that zone rather than only across the system as a whole.
glossary.plain_english: Splitting the property into metered zones, so that when the numbers say water is going missing you know which part of the site it is going missing from. It turns 'we have a leak somewhere' into 'we have a leak in this block'.

glossary.technical: Progressive loss of accuracy in a mechanical water meter with age and cumulative throughput, characteristically most severe at low flow rates. Verified by bench or in-situ accuracy testing against a calibrated standard.
glossary.plain_english: Water meters slow down as they age, and they always err in the same direction — reading less than actually passed through. An old meter quietly tells you that you used less water than you did. That sounds like good news until you remember the City's master meter has no such problem.

glossary.technical: The total volume of water entering the system over the audit period, measured at the point of supply and corrected for master meter accuracy. It is the top line of the water balance; every other figure reconciles against it.
glossary.plain_english: Everything that came onto the property through the pipe, measured at the front door. The whole audit hangs off this number, which is why the accuracy of the meter producing it has to be verified first.

glossary.technical: Water taken by registered customers and for operational purposes, whether billed or unbilled. Unbilled authorized consumption covers uses such as irrigation, line flushing and fire-fighting where these are not metered or charged.
glossary.plain_english: Water that was legitimately used — including the uses nobody sends a bill for, like irrigation, flushing lines and hydrant testing. It is not a loss, but it has to be measured or honestly estimated, otherwise it hides inside the loss figure and makes leakage look worse than it is.
